title: Kathina again
hookLine: the robe offering at the end of the rains

lines: CLOTH AT THE END OF THE RAINS.
cards: Through heat and rain, a monk's robe is worn, slept in, washed, mended, and washed again, until it wears out. A monk owns very few things, so the robe is close to everything he has.
At the end of the rains retreat, lay people in Theravada countries bring cloth for new robes, at a ceremony called Kathina.
You've met it twice: first the story of how the offering began, then the weaving that runs through the night. Today, the robe itself: how it's sewn, and where it goes after it's given.

teach.h: THE PATTERN OF THE RICE FIELDS.
teach.b: Start with the pattern. In the Vinaya, the monastic rulebook, the Buddha is walking through the country of Magadha and looks out over rice fields laid out in strips, with low banks between them.
He asks Ananda whether he could make robes for the monks like that. Ananda can, and does. So the robe isn't one smooth length of cloth.

It's sewn from cut pieces, set out like fields with borders between them. The text gives a reason: cut cloth suits someone who has left home, and nobody would want to steal it. Now follow the robe to its end.

After the Buddha has died, the women of King Udena's palace give Ananda a great gift of robes. The king, puzzled, asks what he'll do with so many. Give them to monks whose robes are worn thin, Ananda says.
And the old robes? Coverlets. The old coverlets?
Mattress covers. Then rugs for the floor, then cloths for wiping feet, then dusters. And the old dusters?
Torn into shreds, beaten into clay, and spread as plaster on the floor. Nothing is wasted. That's what the Kathina cloth walks into.
Not a keepsake for a shelf: a robe worn every day, then passed down the line of uses until the last scrap is part of the floor underfoot. Useful, and meant to be used up.

how: In Theravada countries, lay people offer robe cloth and other useful things to monasteries at Kathina ceremonies after the rains retreat ends, and the monks receive the cloth as a community.

games.why: Ananda follows the cloth all the way down: coverlets, mattress covers, rugs, foot cloths, dusters, and finally clay plaster for the floor.

practice: Bring to mind one useful thing you could give: a warm coat you never wear, a good pan, a tool, an hour of help. Not something precious to admire, but something that will get worn.
See it in someone else's hands, getting scuffed and wearing thin, and let that be the whole gift, with no say in how it's used and no thanks needed.

wordCard.voice: Kathina again. The cloth offered at the end of the rains, sewn into a robe laid out like rice fields, and used until nothing is left. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali kaṭhina: the name of the robe-cloth offering at the end of the rains.

carryVoice: Your line: the robe given. A gift that gets used up has gone where it was needed. Good to see you today.
